Systems lesson 01 · Caching

Cache Workbench

A cache is a small, fast shelf of copies in front of a big, slow store. This lesson builds that idea three ways: watch a machine do it, predict what breaks it, then explain it back.

02

Predict, then run

Each experiment changes one thing. Choose what you expect before running it. Results are averaged over 9,000 simulated requests of the same machine; the figure's starting point is a 67% hit rate.

1. Shorter freshness

Experiment 1 of 5
TTL 60 s → 6 s · a card now leaves the rack ten times sooner
What happens to the share of requests answered from the rack?

A copy only helps if the same record is asked for again before it expires. The most popular record comes back every few requests and still hits, but the next dozen come back every 10 to 30 seconds, after their cards have gone. You trade freshness for trips to the archive.

2. A smaller rack

Experiment 2 of 5
Rack 12 slots → 4 slots · a third of the room
The rack can now hold 4 of the 40 records. The hit rate…

When the rack is full, the card that has gone unused longest is taken out (least recently used). The few popular records are used all the time, so they stay; it is the rarely asked records that get pushed out, and they were rarely hits anyway.

3. No favourites

Experiment 3 of 5
Popular traffic → even traffic · every record equally likely
Same rack, same TTL, but no record is more popular than another. The hit rate…

With even traffic, the chance that the record you want is in the rack is about the share of records the rack holds: 12 of 40 is 30%. Caches pay off because real traffic is uneven: a few things are asked for constantly.

4. The rack is emptied

Experiment 4 of 5
Empty the rack while traffic flows · a deploy, a restart, a flush
Right after the rack is emptied, how long do requests take?

Every request becomes a trip to the archive until the popular cards are back. With skewed traffic that takes only a handful of requests. In a real system those trips arrive all at once, and if they are more than the database can serve, a short refill turns into a queue.

5. A record changes

Experiment 5 of 5
Record #1 is updated in the archive · its card is still in the rack
Of the next reads of #1 answered from the rack, how many show the old version?

The rack has no idea the archive changed. It keeps serving its copy until the TTL runs out. Turning on invalidate on write takes the card out when the record changes, so the next read fetches the new version.

03

Explain it back

Answer out loud or in writing before opening each one. These work well as a pairing exercise: one person explains, the other asks "why?" twice.

Q1In the figure a hit takes 0.7 s and a miss 2.75 s. Why does the average wait depend mostly on the hit rate?
A good answer coversBecause misses are four times as expensive. Average wait = hit rate × 0.7 + (1 − hit rate) × 2.75, so each point of hit rate removes about 0.02 s. Making hits faster would barely help; avoiding misses is what matters.
Q2The rack holds 12 of 40 records but answers about two-thirds of requests. What about the traffic makes that possible, and what would break it?
A good answer coversThe traffic is skewed: a few records get most of the requests, and those stay in the rack. Even traffic breaks it (hit rate falls to about the rack's share, 30%), and so would a key space so large that even the popular part doesn't fit.
Q3A teammate wants TTL = 1 s "so prices are always fresh". What happens, and what would you suggest instead?
A good answer coversMost copies expire before anyone asks again, so the hit rate collapses and the database takes nearly all reads. Keep a longer TTL and invalidate the key when the price changes, so freshness comes from the write, not from expiry.
Q4Invalidate on write fixed the stale reads here. Name one way a stale value can still be served.
A good answer coversA writer that skips the app (a migration, an admin script, another service) doesn't delete the key. Or a race: a reader misses, reads the old row, the writer updates and deletes the key, then the reader stores the old row it read. The TTL is the backstop for both.
Q5Redis restarts during peak traffic. What do you expect in the first seconds, and what would you do before the next deploy?
A good answer coversEvery read misses at once, the database gets more reads than it can serve, requests queue and latency jumps. Warm the cache before switching traffic, add capacity headroom on the database, and consider request coalescing so one miss per key goes to the database.
